claims.claim: Domain names are organized as dot-separated labels in a hierarchy; the rightmost label is the top-level domain in examples such as whois.icann.org.
A party that has registered a domain can create names below it, such as subdomains, subject to the relevant naming rules.
A domain name is distinct from a website and a URL; web hosting or another service is still needed to make an Internet presence functional and accessible.
For generic top-level domains, a registrant may register through an ICANN-accredited registrar, and the registrant-registrar relationship is governed by a registration agreement.
In a typical web URL authority, the domain indicates which web server is requested, while a path identifies a resource location handled by that server.
The generic URI standard treats a host as a subcomponent of authority and describes DNS-oriented registered names as domain labels separated by dots.
